item.title: India Cancels Trains, Floods Capital with Police to Block Protests
item.description:
Law enforcement authorities in India took extraordinary measures Friday to prevent protesters from assembling in the capital, ordering the cancellation of trains bound for Delhi and the suspension of mass transit in the city. They also effectively put several would-be protesters under house arrest.

The moves came in response to a call by the Gen Z movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party for people from all over the country to converge in central Delhi for a protest on Saturday against what they say is a politically motivated purge of India’s voter roll.

Saturday’s rally is to be held at a monument called Jantar Mantar, which has been a protest site for many years, but which security forces are currently blockading.

The restrictions imposed by law enforcement authorities led India’s highest court to issue a rare emergency order on Friday afternoon, urging the government to reconsider the limits and offer an alternative space for a protest. Responding to an appeal from an opposition party politician, the court also said the city’s metro service should not be shut down completely.

“You have to prevent certain things,” the chief justice of the Supreme Court, Surya Kant, said.

“But that does not mean you should use a hammer to kill a fly,” he added.

(It was Mr. Kant who unwittingly gave rise to the cockroach movement, when he likened unemployed youth to cockroaches. In response, Abhijeet Dipke, then a graduate student living in Boston, wrote on social media: “What if all cockroaches come together?” It gave birth to the Cockroach Janta Party.)

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has not commented on this week’s protests.

Saturday’s planned protest follows a week of nationwide demonstrations demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of India’s election commission, a body that was long held in high regard for running fair polls but has recently come under intense public criticism because of the voter roll revision. That exercise to clean up voter lists began last summer and ended up eliminating 130 million names. Critics say it is an effort to entrench Mr. Modi’s power.

In the capital, opposition parties and other activist groups have held daily protests for the last week, only to be aggressively restrained by police and then detained. On Friday, videos spread on social media of police officers pulling young would-be protesters from trains bound for Delhi in various parts of the country.

There was a heavy police presence in central Delhi on Friday. Around Jantar Mantar, tall yellow police barricades were chained together. Loudspeakers were erected at traffic circles, playing announcements warning people not to gather. “Violation may lead to legal action against you,” the announcements said.

India has long prided itself as a thriving democracy, even as space for dissent has shrunk in Mr. Modi’s 12-year tenure.

The government’s heavy-handed efforts this week go considerably further than recent attempts to stop anti-government agitation. This summer’s protests by the Cockroach party uncorked a generation’s rage over a dysfunctional college entrance exam system and won the rare ouster of a government minister. The government did not stop the protesters from gathering this summer but responded with force.

On Friday, Delhi police said they had denied permission for the rally, saying the organizers had not asked for permission sufficiently in advance and broke rules the last time they protested, without offering evidence of which rules they broke. In a news conference, Nupur Prasad, a senior police official, said “reasonable preventive restrictions” had been put in place. She warned legal action against those who violate the order.

Ashutosh Ranka, a leader of the Cockroach party, said in a voice note to The Times on Friday evening that the protest would go on. “The government is in complete panic,” he said in the voice note. “They don’t know how to deal with peaceful protesters, and that’s why they are resorting to absolutely dictatorial measures.”

“It’s a shame that in the world’s largest democracy you have to protest to even go and protest at a designated protest site,” he added, referring to Jantar Mantar.

Police tactics have succeeded, to an extent, in preventing protesters from reaching Delhi.

Kunal Choudhary, 26, was planning to lead a delegation of around 30 people to Delhi from a town three hours away by bus. But on Thursday evening, police officers showed up at his home and have not left, he said, offering no warrant for his arrest.

“They showed me a WhatsApp group where there was a list with my name also. They were given orders to go to all those people’s homes,” he said.

As he narrated the events by speakerphone, a police officer, Manvendra Singh, listened in, identifying himself on the call. He refused to say why he was there, only that Mr. Choudhary would be detained at home through Saturday evening.

Mr. Choudhary’s mother, Mitika, served the police officer tea and Oreo cookies for breakfast. “My mother is used to this now. She used to be quite scared,” he said. It was the third time in a month police had shown up at his house.

item.title: Navi Pillay, South African Jurist, Is Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize
item.description:
A South African lawyer with a long record in human rights work, including leading a U.N. commission that said Israel had committed genocide, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday, a decision that drew Israel’s condemnation and underscored the country’s deep isolation on the world stage.

The lawyer, Navanethem Pillay, known as Navi, has worked for decades on human rights issues, defending anti-apartheid activists like the future president and Nobel laureate Nelson Mandela. Over the years, she has variously served as a top U.N. official and as a judge on the International Criminal Court and a tribunal investigating genocide in Rwanda.

But it was Ms. Pillay’s work last year on a U.N. commission on Israel that made the Nobel committee’s announcement on Friday an intensely political decision, as it put the prize in the middle of one of the world’s most divisive issues.

That commission said that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a finding that Israel rejected.

Announcing the award, the Nobel committee did not explicitly mention Gaza, instead citing Ms. Pillay’s long career in human rights and a global shift toward “power politics” that had undermined respect for law and justice. The committee chair, Jorgen Watne Frydnes, called the award “a message to those who are attacking” international law.

Ms. Pillay, 85, is “one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said, calling her “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.”

The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, quickly denounced the committee in a statement, calling its members misguided and saying it had “lost its moral compass.” It also condemned Ms. Pillay’s work, accusing her of being prejudiced against Jews.

The Israeli foreign ministry went further, calling the Nobel decision a “grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.”

After learning she had won the award, Ms. Pillay, speaking at a conference of human rights lawyers in Nuremberg, Germany, said she had tried to hew only to the law and facts in her career, not politics.

“Why would you need courage to speak the truth?” she said. “You interpret the law, you look at all the facts. So it’s an impartial, you know, impartial decision-making.”

Her work on Israel and Gaza, though, was “an important part of the reasoning why she received the prize,” Mr. Frydnes, the Nobel committee chair, told reporters.

President Trump, who has been a staunch supporter of Israel and has openly angled to win the Nobel Peace Prize himself, did not immediately address Friday’s award. He did, however, share a post on his social media platform that called Ms. Pillay “an unabashed hater of America and Israel” and said that it was Mr. Trump who deserved the prize.

After receiving the news at the conference in Nuremberg, Ms. Pillay was applauded by more than a hundred fellow attendees, a video posted by the Amnesty International head, Agnès Callamard, showed.

“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” Ms. Pillay joked, apparently referring to last year’s winner, María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader who presented her medal to the U.S. president in January.

At a brief news conference, Ms. Pillay mused that “perhaps it was meant to be” that she had received the news in Nuremberg, a city whose famous postwar trials of Nazi leaders were foundational to creating the modern international justice system.

“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said. Such efforts, she said, were “particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court,” which the Trump administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick.”

Born to a family of Indian Tamil origin, the daughter of a homemaker and a bus driver, Ms. Pillay was one of seven children who grew up in poverty in the city of Durban, on South Africa’s east coast. She came of age in a segregated city, attending a school for Indian South Africans.

As a teenager, Ms. Pillay said, she experienced apartheid’s daily injustices and witnessed the violent crackdown by police forces and vigilantes on Black South African protesters and their supporters.

“The government was oppressive, the laws were oppressive and the courts cooperated with these laws,” she said in a video published by the I.C.C. in 2017. “We had no remedies, and as a 15-year-old, I wished that we could appeal to a higher system of law, a higher institution, so that we, the victims, can get justice.”

Ms. Pillay pursued a law degree and later defended imprisoned anti-apartheid activists, including Nelson Mandela, many of whom faced terrorism charges and placed under surveillance. After the end of apartheid, Ms. Pillay became a judge on the High Court in South Africa, where she championed women’s rights and equality.

Soon, Ms. Pillay was drawn into international human rights crises. In 1995, Mr. Mandela — then South Africa’s president — appointed her as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

Ms. Pillay is the fifth South African to be awarded the peace prize, after Mr. Mandela, the activist Albert Luthuli, former President F.W. de Klerk and Desmond Tutu, the cleric who helped bring down apartheid.

One of Ms. Pillay’s contributions to international law was her pioneering work on the gravity of sexual violence during the Rwanda conflict. In a trial at the tribunal, she pushed from the bench to define rape of women and children as a weapon of war.

In 1998, when the tribunal found a former Rwandan mayor guilty of genocide, it was the first time that rape had been defined as part of genocide. Sexual violence has since been integrated in international law as a potential war crime, a crime against humanity or an act of genocide.

Two decades later, in 2019, Ms. Pillay served as an ad hoc judge on the International Court of Justice in a case in which Myanmar was accused of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority.

Even as her work expanded beyond South Africa, she remained a prominent voice for human rights in the country, speaking out against anti-immigrant violence that flared in Durban in 2015 and chiding the South African government for having considered leaving the I.C.C. in 2016.

This year’s selection is the latest in a line of decisions by the Norwegian Nobel Committee that have carried political weight.

The year before awarding the prize to Ms. Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader, the committee honored Nihon Hidankyo, a Japanese organization representing atomic bomb survivors, many of whom have campaigned for nuclear disarmament. In 2023, the prize went to Narges Mohammadi, Iran’s most prominent human rights activist.

item.title: Large Earthquake in Panama Sets Off Tsunami Alert
item.description:
An earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.7 hit the Central American nation of Panama on Friday, shaking buildings in Panama City and prompting evacuations, according to the U.S. Geological Survey and videos posted on social media. Tsunami alerts affecting the region followed.

The quake hit about 1:56 p.m. Eastern time, according to the U.S.G.S. It was centered about nine miles southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a town in the country’s southern Azuero Peninsula. It was followed by at least three strong aftershocks in the following hour.

In Panama City, the capital, northeast of the earthquake’s epicenter, buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets, according to video footage posted on social media. About 2 million people live in the capital region.

The quake prompted the U.S. Pacific Tsunami Warning Center to issue alerts along the Pacific Coast of several Central American countries. Hazardous waves that could reach up to 10 feet above tide levels are possible in Panama. The center said waves up to a foot above normal were possible in countries with Pacific Ocean coastlines from Ecuador to New Zealand, the center said.

No immediate threats were reported for the United States.

Aurelio Martínez, a spokesman for the Panamanian national police, said in a brief phone interview that there damage had been reported in the interior of the country, including in the Veraguas Province in Central Panama. But he said that it was too soon to tell how much structural damage the country had sustained, and if there were any injuries or deaths.

The U.S. Embassy in Panama said there were no initial reports of injuries among its staff or at the embassy.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

Jack Nicas and John Keefe contributed reporting.

View the location of the quake’s epicenter and shake area.

item.title: Blocked by Police, India’s Youth Voice Their Fury
item.description:
Tanmay Koli, 20, rode a train for two days by himself to come to his nation’s capital. He found his way to a Sikh temple to sit for a while and eat. Then he headed out into the streets of New Delhi with two other young men, who, like him, had come by train from their own hometowns far away.

On Saturday, all three of them, strangers until just a few hours ago, sat together on a curb staring at barricades and a phalanx of security forces. They were nervous, they said, but they wanted to be here.

“They’re stealing votes,” Mr. Koli, said. He had come from Pune, a city to the south.

“Democracy is not safe,” said his new friend, a 28-year-old man who, fearing reprisal, gave only his first name, Om. He had traveled from Chandigarh, a city to the north.

They were among the scores of young Indians who arrived in Delhi to protest the erasure of millions of people from voter rolls. To keep them away, the police canceled several trains, closed dozens of metro stations and filled the center of the capital with yellow barricades, buses and security forces bearing shields and batons.

In interviews and in social media posts, the would-be protesters, many of them supporters or leaders of the Gen Z-focused Cockroach Janta Party, expressed outrage and frustration at the heavy-handed measures to snuff out the demonstration before it began.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the party, was intercepted by the police as soon as he landed in New Delhi on Saturday, he and the group said. On Instagram, he uploaded video of officers boarding the aircraft to detain him. So, too, were his two fellow Cockroach leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, the party said in a statement.

“This is dictatorship,” Mr. Dipke is heard saying as an officer approached his seat.

Ratna Singh, who leads the Cockroach Janta Party’s legal team, said more than two dozen police officers surrounded her car, trapping her inside. In a video shared by the group, Ms. Singh says the police told her they wanted to take her to her house and hold her there. When she asked them for a warrant, the police said: “We have orders from above.”

“I am not getting out of the car, and they are not leaving this space,” she says in the video.

Nearly 300 would-be protesters were holed up on Saturday inside a Sikh temple about a mile and a half from Jantar Mantar, the site where the demonstration was supposed to be held. Most of them had arrived during the night, but the road to the site was barricaded by the police.

“I am here to protest against not just the corruption with our votes, but also the corruption in the education system,” said Lucky, 23, who would only identify himself by his first name for fear of reprisal. He had traveled 14 hours by train from his village in Bihar, a state to the east.

“I don’t think they will shoot us or kill us,” he said. “At most, they will take us to jail — and I am ready for that.”

Closer to Jantar Mantar, a group of women sat on the curb, waiting for other protesters to arrive.

“Look at the situation, how our country is treating us,” Nada Haseen, 22, said. “We are asking for our basic right — to vote, and for that we are fighting, in a very nonviolent form of protest, which is allowed in our constitution.”

“Aren’t we children of this nation?” she added.

item.title: Quebec Independence Is Unlikely, but Some Will Still Dream
item.description:
Lambert Léveillé taught high school math forever in Beloeil, Quebec. So it wasn’t surprising that middle-aged men came up to greet him as I interviewed him in the parking lot of the elementary school where he had just voted last Monday.

Léveillé, 80, may golf a lot these days, but he still turns to math to understand the world, including the provincial election in Quebec.

“The latest poll gave the Parti Québécois 29 percent,” he told me. “They’ll win. But with five parties in the mix, the vote will be split, and so it’ll be a minority government.”

The retired math teacher’s analysis proved correct when the ballots were counted later that day. The separatist Parti Québécois beat the other parties by winning 59 seats, short of the 64 seats needed for a majority in the 127-seat provincial legislature.

Its leader, premier-elect Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, 49, was the first leader of the separatist party in a generation to promise a referendum on independence if his party won. His promise roused the party’s base. But since independence remains deeply unpopular in Quebec — 70 percent are against it — he tried to ease concerns among other voters by pledging to hold a referendum only after Donald Trump leaves office in 2029 and the economy stabilizes.

[Read: Parti Québécois Returns to Power, Reviving Quebec Sovereignty Push]

The numbers point to the obstacles he faces. In Quebec, minority governments have lasted less than two years on average, so St-Pierre Plamondon could be out office before Trump. He lacks a popular mandate, as his party won only 28 percent of the popular vote, the lowest on record.

With only a minority, he would need to persuade at least five lawmakers from opposition parties to join his call for a referendum. But the second and third biggest parties, the Quebec Liberal Party and the Conservative Party of Quebec, are staunchly against independence. The fourth party, Québec Solidaire, is separatist, with a vision of an independent Quebec as a collection of Québécois, immigrants and 11 Indigenous groups who prioritize climate change. This view might resonate in the nine left-leaning, diverse districts it won, all but one in Quebec’s two biggest cities, Montreal and Quebec City, but perhaps not in the Parti Québécois heartland.

The Parti Québécois was shut out of Quebec City and won only two seats out of 27 on the island of Montreal. But it swept the French-speaking suburban and rural areas populated mostly by the French Québécois, or French Canadians, who, historically, have been the main supporters of the party’s fight for an independent Quebec built on the French Québécois identity and culture.

Last Monday, I drove out to two suburban districts east of Montreal where two high-profile incumbents — sitting ministers of the Coalition Avenir Quebec — were at risk of losing.

A small city with detached homes on tree-lined streets, Beloeil is in a predominantly francophone district, Borduas, traditionally a Parti Québécois stronghold but held for the past eight years by the Coalition Avenir Quebec. On Monday, the district overwhelmingly swung back to the Parti Québécois.

Still, few voters I met in Beloeil expressed interest in a referendum. No one was strongly against independence, but what I heard over and over again was that the math wasn’t there anymore.

Quebec had changed so much since the unsuccessful referendums of 1980 and 1995. Back then, an independent Quebec was perhaps the final outcome of the self-determination of the French Québécois, a people who had liberated themselves from the grips of the Roman Catholic Church and the province’s English-speaking minority.

[Read: Separatists Are Set to Win Quebec’s Election. What Will It Mean for Independence?]

Today, they are better educated, richer and, polls show, have little interest in independence. Equally important, the province’s other communities, especially the growing immigrant population, are decidedly against independence.

“We know that there’s only 30 percent of the population that’s interested in a referendum,” Léveillé, the retired math teacher, said, referring to polls. “At some point, you have to be able to see things clearly. There’s not a heck of a lot of anglophones who are going to vote for independence, and immigrants feel more Canadian.”

“So independence is very unlikely, mathematically speaking,’’ he said, “even though it’s nice to dream.’’

To Patrice Desjardins, 47, the numbers didn’t add up either. A small construction business owner, Desjardins said he might have voted for independence if he had been old enough in 1995.

Today, he felt that the cost of holding a referendum — cited at 130 million Canadian dollars by St-Pierre Plamondon during the campaign — would be better spent on other things like health care.

“It’s pointless to hold a referendum,” Desjardins said. “Maybe there was a chance years ago to become independent, but today the chances are becoming increasingly slim. So it’s not because I’m against it, but because it’s not possible.”

“It’s already too late,” he added

And then there was Dominique Tessier, 68, a lifelong die-hard separatist whose support for independence grew out of his family history.

“I’m Québécois, francophone, my mother and father went to church,” he said. “I know our history.”

When he played hockey as a boy, elbows flew against the “anglophones” of Otterburn Park, a city across the river from Beloeil that used to be home to English speakers. He came of age, politically, in the 1970s, when Quebec francophones led the construction of the province’s giant hydroelectric dams and when the Parti Québécois first took power under its charismatic leader, René Lévesque. He sent his three children to university.

If there is a third time, Tessier said he would vote “yes” again for independence — even though he, too, felt that perhaps the time had passed

Tessier never taught math, but he knew his numbers. He worked in commercial real estate for years. Now, he drove a school bus for 20 hours a week in Brossard, a diverse suburb just south of Montreal.

“There aren’t any Québécois there anymore, just immigrants,” he said, adding that immigrants would not share the history that had led to his commitment to independence.

“Will Quebec separate one day?” he said “Probably not.”

Probably not, mathematically speaking. Dreaming, though, was something else.

Norimitsu Onishi is a Montreal-based correspondent for The New York Times covering Canada.

Vjsoa Isai, a Toronto-based reporter for The Times, and the photographer Cole Burston, went into the operating room at Toronto General Hospital earlier this year to see how doctors there have been using artificial intelligence in their surgical practices. Dr. Amin Madani, an endocrine and acute care surgeon, is training an A.I. model to think like the best surgeons, and testing the bounds of what A.I. can do in the operating room.

Read the full article.

The Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday by the Swedish Academy, which cited “her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.” We looked at why Ms. Carson is the easiest difficult poet, and why Princeton, which denied her tenure, celebrated her this week.

Canada will reverse its plan to allow people whose sole condition is a mental illness to seek medically assisted death, the government announced on Wednesday, abandoning a move to expand access to these patients, Vjosa Isai reported.

From Opinion: Dr. Gary Rodin and Dr. Madeline Li, professors of psychiatry at the University of Toronto, wrote that Canada’s system for assisted death is no longer an option of last resort.

The U.S. authorities arrested a 30-year-old Washington State resident on Tuesday on charges of conspiring to commit a school shooting in rural British Columbia, eight months after a Canadian teenager killed eight people, Vjosa Isai reported.

The Can-Am Spyder, a three-wheel roadster, has a devoted fan base across the United States. Now it’s a casualty in the trade war with Canada.

George Gillett Jr., an entrepreneur whose best known acquisitions were in sports — ski resorts, the Miami Dolphins, the Harlem Globetrotters, the Montreal Canadiens, the Liverpool soccer club and a NASCAR racing team — died on Sept. 22 at the age of 87.

A medical plane, traveling from Bermuda to Boston with four Canadians on board and two people picked up in Bermuda, lost contact shortly after 1 a.m. last Saturday. The U.S. Coast Guard found debris off the coast of Nantucket, Mass. More on the plane and the victims.

The F.B.I. has arrested a Canadian citizen in Pennsylvania on suspicion of being a co-conspirator behind a computer hack of sensitive information about thousands of F.B.I. employees.

How are we doing?We’re eager to have your thoughts about this newsletter and events in Canada in general. Please send them to nytcanada@nytimes.com.

item.title: Attacker in FlyDubai Flight Meant to Crash Into Israeli Airport, Emiratis Say
item.description:
Emirati investigators said on Friday that the co-pilot who attacked the captain of a FlyDubai flight last week had developed extremist Islamist views over several years and had intended to carry out a Sept. 11-inspired suicide crash into Israel’s biggest airport.

The details, disclosed by the Emirati attorney general, offered the most comprehensive official account so far of the co-pilot’s motives and preparation. The report also deepened questions about how signs of his radicalization were missed before he was allowed to fly such a sensitive route.

More than 170 passengers, mostly Israelis, were on FlyDubai Flight 1073 last week when the co-pilot began attacking the pilot with the plane’s crash ax and then tried to crash the airliner. The pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, managed to unlock the cockpit door, and passengers were able to subdue the assailant, narrowly averting a catastrophe.

Backup pilots were on board and ultimately stabilized the plane, bringing it to an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

The Emirati attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot, a 29-year-old Omani national, had planned to crash the plane into the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life.”

The Emirati statement did not identify the co-pilot, but people familiar with the investigation have said that his name is Hamam al-Hammami, and that his embrace of radical Islamist views prompted the Omani authorities to scrutinize him earlier.

The Emirati investigation found that the co-pilot had begun a “drift towards extremism and terrorism” almost a decade ago, while he was a student in Melbourne, Australia. The Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology said in a statement that the co-pilot was enrolled at the university between 2015 and 2017 but did not complete his engineering degree.

While in Australia, Mr. al-Hammami developed a fascination with extremist literature and online content “glorifying terrorist organizations and suicide operations” the Emirati statement said. He also “received support” from groups related to the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Islamist movement, according to the statement, without elaborating further.

Taking inspiration from the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, and takfir ideology — a view that effectively allows one Muslim to declare another an apostate — the co-pilot became increasingly interested in a similar attack, the Emirati statement said.

He confessed to the authorities that following through on that vision was “linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation,” according to investigators. Before coming to FlyDubai in January 2026, he was employed by Oman Air for four years and spent a brief stint at Royal Maroc Air, a Moroccan airline, the investigation found.

The co-pilot told the authorities that he acted alone, investigators said, though they added that were still looking into that question. To prepare for the operation, he had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the route, consumed more “material promoting terrorism” and trained in boxing, the Emirati statement said.

But the disclosure left open questions about how Mr. al-Hammami was cleared to fly such a sensitive route. It is unclear whether Omani investigators had shared their concerns with security officials in Israel, the United Arab Emirates — where the flight originated — or with the airline.

Mr. Al Shamsi said the co-pilot “had met the professional and security requirements for employment” at FlyDubai, including completing required checks and providing a certificate of “good conduct.” He added that none of the steps revealed “any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot.”

The plane’s passengers were mostly Israelis, some of whom said the crisis evoked the feelings of dread they had last felt on Oct. 7, 2023, during the Hamas-led attack on Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

After the failed attack on the plane, two posts appeared on a LinkedIn profile bearing Mr. al-Hammami’s name. One depicted a photo of Ayman al-Zawahri, who led Al Qaeda after Osama bin Laden’s death and was killed by the United States in 2022. It was not clear who made the posts or whether they had been scheduled in advance to be published.

Victoria Kim contributed reporting.

item.title: As Putin Wages Shadow War, Europe Looks for a Way to Hit Back
item.description:
Russia is escalating its campaign of sabotage in NATO countries, trying to break European support for Kyiv — and Europe is struggling to respond.

European officials say they do not expect a major Russian invasion of a NATO country; in that sense, traditional deterrence has worked. But countries are grappling with how best to counter this heightened pattern of Russian attacks. What officials say they fear most is that, by accident or by intention, one of those attacks will cause a significant loss of life.

Moscow is “trying to break the will to support Ukraine and trying in a broader sense to change the security architecture of Europe,” said David Cattler, a former NATO intelligence official now at the Center for European Policy Analysis, a Washington think tank. Operationally, he said, the Russians are using tools “that are hard to attribute, that they believe are big enough to matter and yet small enough not to trigger” a larger war.

Internally, the debate among European officials, they said, is whether and how to retaliate by taking the fight to Russia. The first response should be to maintain calm and not fall into a Russian trap by overreacting, said Camille Grand, a former senior NATO official, while not being so complacent as to ignore reality. The Russian campaign is a continuation of a pattern, he said, but “the growth in the number and nature of the events is significant, and the dangerous nature of them.”

Europe is trying to increase deterrence against hybrid warfare — aggressive actions that fall short of direct military conflict — on three levels: first, by calling out Russia’s attacks and blaming the Kremlin directly; second, by increasing societal awareness and building stronger defenses around potential targets; and third, by imposing consequences on Moscow, whether overt or covert, with clear messaging to President Vladimir V. Putin.

“Any attack should be clearly linked to a concrete measure of response,” said Linas Kojala of the Geopolitics and Security Studies Center, a research group in Lithuania. “To make that work,” he added, “governments would need to have funding and legal authority prepared in advance, so the response is not delayed by a new political debate after every incident.”

That presumes collective European agreement on responses to unpredictable attacks that could quickly lead to war, decisions that countries have traditionally reserved to themselves. But producing such a consensus, as Mr. Cattler, the former NATO official, said dryly, “can be quite a challenge.”

Recent incidents directly attributed to Russia or thought ordered by Moscow include strikes on railroad infrastructure in Poland, a Russian frigate’s firing flares at a Danish helicopter, sabotage at factories, incursions by Russian reconnaissance drones and plots to kill executives of European armaments companies.

While many episodes are hard to pin on Russia, Berlin directly attributed to Moscow a recent explosive-laden but faulty drone at the Leipzig-Halle airport in eastern Germany, found near Ukrainian transport planes. The failed attack — the drone was discovered by an airport employee — was among several incidents that have spurred fresh warnings across Europe.

The drone at Leipzig-Halle marked a shift, both for Russian risk-taking and for Germany’s willingness to point the finger at Moscow.

Claudia Major, a defense expert with the German Marshall Fund, said that Mr. Putin wanted “not only to show that support for Ukraine has a cost, but to undermine the trust of the populace that a democratic state can protect them.” Russia’s aim in Ukraine is not only territorial, she added, but also “to show that the West doesn’t hold together and can be undermined from within.”

The Russian president has been more explicit lately in warning NATO countries supporting Ukraine that they can be targeted. Russia is also suspected of trying to influence key elections in France, Italy, Poland and Spain, where far-right and pro-Russian parties are mounting significant challenges, European officials note.

Inducing fear in adversaries is a longstanding element of Russian strategy, said Hanna Notte, a Russia expert who has recently published a book about Mr. Putin’s effort to defeat the West called “We Shall Outlast Them.”

Ms. Notte noted that Sergey A. Karaganov, a hard-line Russian analyst, wrote in 2024 that for Moscow to prevail against the West, “There must be fear.” Another prominent analyst who came to support the war, Dmitri V. Trenin, she recalled, has written, “Where there is no fear, there is no security.”

Mr. Putin deterred former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. from doing more for Ukraine by threatening nuclear escalation, said Keir Giles, a Russia scholar at Chatham House, a research group in London. Under President Trump, Mr. Giles said, “It’s not the U.S. that needs to be deterred or coerced, but Europe.”

NATO is already increasing its conventional deterrence, conducting more and larger exercises along the Russian border. Europe’s efforts to increase deterrence against hybrid warfare are less advanced and less visible.

The region is increasingly focused on attribution, with leaders and intelligence agencies becoming more explicit about Russian responsibility and intentions, using words like “kinetic” rather than “hybrid,” to imply that this is a more active kind of war.

Europe is also investing heavily in protecting airports, critical infrastructure, railway junctions and important factories. Some countries, such as Denmark, Finland and Poland, are preparing citizens for potential warfare, with warnings and public-service notices. NATO countries can count such efforts toward the alliance goal of spending 5 percent of gross domestic product on defense by 2034.

Such action is necessary but cannot guard against accidents, real or intentional, that kill people and leave Western countries at a loss on how to respond, analysts said.

Resilience still leaves Russia with the initiative, Mr. Kojala said. “The response has to go beyond protection,” he noted. “It should target the networks behind these operations — identify and indict Russian intelligence officers, disrupt the recruitment and payment of local proxies.”

That is the more delicate third part of Europe’s response, which is to impose costs on Russian behavior. To identify Moscow as a culprit and not impose commensurate consequences shows weakness and encourages more attacks, said Mr. Cattler, the former NATO intelligence official. But the messaging must also be careful and collective, he said, rather than a single country’s response to a single act.

Analysts suggested, for instance, that cyber capabilities could be used to shut down a Russian town or the Moscow subway as a warning message. And if the worry is about a drone or missile strike, deliberate or otherwise, NATO countries could institute forward air defense, including over Ukrainian territory, to shoot down threats heading toward NATO territory, as Radoslaw Sikorski, the foreign minister of Poland, has urged.

While Washington can send a powerful private message to Moscow through its intelligence chief or a presidential phone call, Europe has no single person who can speak for the bloc, said Max Bergmann of the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.

“Europe hasn’t integrated on defense and foreign policy so really can’t convey coherent messages,” he noted.

Ivo Daalder, a former U.S. ambassador to NATO now at Harvard’s Belfer Center, noted efforts in the European Union to propose a security protocol for consultations on incidents of hybrid war, similar to NATO’s Article 4.

But Europe “needs a menu, not another meeting,” Mr. Daalder said. NATO, he added, is better prepared than the European Union to create a list of prepackaged collective responses to hybrid warfare, and the alliance has a command structure to carry them out.

That, he suggested, is a message Russia is more likely to understand.

item.title: Ukrainian Drones Close Moscow Airports as Putin Flies Back to Russia
item.description:
A Ukrainian drone barrage shut down Moscow’s airports for hours on Friday, as several Russian government aircraft reportedly bringing President Vladimir V. Putin and his aides back from a summit in Turkmenistan were returning to the Russian capital.

Data from FlightRadar24 showed that the Russian government jets either circled Moscow or diverted to St. Petersburg.

It isn’t clear which jet was carrying Mr. Putin, who had arrived in Turkmenbashi, a Caspian Sea port city, on Thursday evening for a summit of former Soviet states.

The Russian leader has multiple Il-96-300PU planes which, like Air Force One, allow him to operate a command-and-control center from the air during a nuclear conflict. Known as the “Flying Kremlin,” the presidential jet flies along with identical aircraft that function as decoys to protect Mr. Putin’s security.

According to FlightRadar24 data, three such planes took off from Turkmenbashi on Friday afternoon, when the Russian state news agency Tass reported that the Russian leader had left the city and boarded a plane for the trip home.

The first two aircraft made abnormal looping maneuvers as they entered the airspace around Moscow, because Ukrainian drones had forced the capital’s four airports to shut down. The third plane, which had taken off after the other two, diverted to St. Petersburg and later flew to Moscow.

Video footage showed Mr. Putin disembarking in Turkmenistan for the summit on Thursday from a presidential jet with the tail number 96025 written underneath its wing. That is the aircraft that, according to FlightRadar24 data, diverted to St. Petersburg.

It is unclear, however, if Mr. Putin took the same plane on the way back from the summit. Nor has the government indicated whether he has returned to Moscow.

Airport closures in the Russian capital have become a common occurrence because of barrages of Ukrainian drones, and there was no indication whether the latest one was timed to the Russian president’s travel. On Friday, hundreds of flights were canceled or delayed, with all four of the capital’s airports suspending flights.

Commercial flights haven’t operated in Ukraine since Mr. Putin invaded in 2022 because of the danger posed by Russian missiles and drones in Ukrainian airspace.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine accused Russia of interfering with his travel when his plane was grounded last month in Moldova on account of a Russian drone entering the country’s airspace.

The Kremlin didn’t respond to reports that the Ukrainian drone attack had interfered with the Russian leader’s travel.

Not long after Mr. Putin returned to Russia, President Trump announced a deal with the Kremlin to lift Russia’s ban on exporting diesel fuel.

Mr. Trump said he had reached the deal after a “highly successful discussion” with Mr. Putin. The U.S. Treasury announced that it would temporarily issue a sanctions waiver on Russian diesel being released to the global market.

The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has driven up the price of oil and diesel, a liability for Mr. Trump and Republicans heading into the midterm elections next month.

Though Russia is usually one of the world’s largest exporters of diesel fuel, months of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries created fuel shortages, prompting Moscow to ban diesel exports this summer, exacerbating the global supply crunch.

item.title: A Deadly Firefight Exposes Erik Prince’s New Shadow War in Congo
item.description:
The hasty evacuation of a former Green Beret who was badly wounded during a firefight in the Democratic Republic of Congo last month, has opened a window into the latest mercenary deployment by Erik Prince, the high-profile American military contractor.

The former Green Beret, Tim Kennedy, who is also known for his career in mixed martial arts and frequent appearances on Fox News, was shot several times during intense fighting in Congo’s eastern highlands, where government forces have been battling a powerful, Rwanda-backed rebel group.

An elite ex-soldier from New Zealand who previously served with his country’s Special Air Service unit was killed. Six people briefed on different aspects of the ambush and subsequent evacuation spoke to The New York Times on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the operation.

What brought both men to Congo was their employment by Mr. Prince, the founder of Blackwater Worldwide, a company notorious for a civilian massacre in Iraq in 2007. For years, Mr. Prince has sought opportunities in resource-rich countries plagued by conflict, mostly in Africa. Now his interests are expanding in Congo, where the government has hired foreign help to fend off the rebel advance in the east, while also trying to curry favor with the Trump administration.

To advance its goals, Kinshasa has turned to Mr. Prince, a prominent supporter of President Trump, giving him a central role in one of Africa’s most intractable conflicts.

Details of Mr. Prince’s operations in Congo were provided to The Times by a dozen current and former officials from the United States, Congo, Europe and other African countries, as well as U.N. officials, military contractors and some of Mr. Prince’s own employees. All spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss military casualties or confidential business arrangements.

Mr. Prince declined to comment for this article, as did a spokesman for Vectus Global, the company that leads his operations in Congo.

Mr. Prince’s growing influence in Congo comes as the Trump administration seeks a new toehold for American companies in the country’s lucrative mining industry, where China’s dominance over critical minerals like cobalt is a source of growing concern in Washington. Last December the United States and Congo signed an agreement granting preferential access to American mining interests in Congo, which many Congolese officials privately called a “peace for minerals” deal.

In late 2024, Mr. Prince signed a wide-ranging contract to provide security and mining services to President Félix Tshisekedi’s government. The contract was worth hundreds of millions of dollars over five years, although it is unclear how much has been paid out, said a former U.S. official who worked on regional diplomacy.

Since then, Mr. Prince has supplied drones and mercenaries to help Congo fight the M23, the rebel group backed by Rwanda, and has even moved into taxation. His company in Congo employs about 100 people in a drive to recoup some of the estimated $3 billion in taxes that Congo loses every year from fraud in the mining sector.

The tax effort is led by a former French Foreign Legion soldier who works from a gleaming new financial center in the capital, Kinshasa. Speaking on the condition of anonymity, an employee of Mr. Prince described plans to digitize mining records, tackle widespread fraud and curb what he called the “blatant looting” of Congolese resources by criminal syndicates that include Chinese mining companies.

Mr. Prince’s employee likened the anticorruption drive to that of Eliot Ness, the Prohibition-era law enforcement officer who aggressively went after the crime boss Al Capone’s bootlegging empire.

The employee said the tax effort is going well. But in the rugged highlands 1,000 miles to the east, where Congo’s war is being fought, Mr. Prince’s other mission has been stymied by setbacks and casualties — not for the first time, say his critics.

“Among mercenaries, especially in Africa, Prince is derided because he has zero successful missions,” said Sean McFate, a former private military contractor who is currently a fellow at The Atlantic Council.

For the past year, mercenaries employed by Mr. Prince have been based at an airfield in Kalemie, a town on the western shore of Lake Tanganyika in eastern Congo, several of the current and former officials said. Drone pilots from Colombia and Ukraine, contracted by Mr. Prince, carried out strikes against the M23, the most powerful of more than 100 armed groups operating in Congo. Last January, Mr. Prince’s forces helped the Congolese recapture the key city of Uvira.

But as fighting intensified recently in the nearby Minembwe Highlands, where remote villages nestle amid steep slopes, Mr. Prince’s employees were drawn into a vicious fight. One battle early last month led to the deaths of several Colombian contractors, according to a person briefed on the incident and a report seen by The Times.

Then on Sept. 17, a second group of mercenaries accompanying Congolese soldiers, this time including Mr. Kennedy, was caught in the deadly ambush.

What exactly happened is unclear. One person close to Mr. Prince, briefed on the incident, would only say that it was a “long ordeal,” which was exacerbated by a lack of support from Congolese forces.

When it was over, Mr. Kennedy had been shot multiple times and several others were dead, including Justin Conaglen, a former special operations soldier from New Zealand. Asked about Mr. Conaglen’s death, a spokesman for New Zealand’s foreign ministry said it was “providing support in this case” but declined to provide further information.

After the ambush, Mr. Prince’s officials began to search for air transport options to evacuate the dead and wounded, the people briefed on the incident said. Mr. Kennedy was rushed to Burundi and then South Africa for treatment at the private Milpark hospital in Johannesburg.

Mr. Kennedy has since been flown back to the United States, where he is recovering at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, a flagship facility that primarily treats active-duty troops, friends and officials said.

The Pentagon declined to comment, and Mr. Kennedy did not respond to questions.

Known for his dual career in the military and professional sports, Mr. Kennedy served as a Green Beret and competed in the Ultimate Fighting Championship until he retired from professional fighting in 2017. He has hosted shows for the History and Discovery channels, published an autobiography, “Scars and Stripes,” and has drawn criticism for making provocative statements about the nature of war on podcasts and TV.

Accusations last year that Mr. Kennedy had exaggerated his military awards prompted the Maryland National Guard to investigate. He publicly apologized for having “unintentionally misstated aspects of my military service.”

Mr. Conaglen took unpaid leave from the New Zealand military in March, before formally leaving the service in August, a spokesman for his country’s military said in an email.

Originally from New Zealand’s North Island, he competed in endurance sports and high-altitude mountaineering, and was part-owner of a holiday rental business in Raglan, a surfing town known for its black-sand beaches.

His remains were returned to New Zealand, where they were cremated on Oct. 1 after a memorial at a rugby club in the small town of Taipa.

Western mercenaries have long been a sensitive subject in Congo, where hundreds of European fighters joined an effort by the Katanga region to secede in the 1960s. Many Congolese also remember the C.I.A.’s role in the overthrow of their country’s first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, who was later executed by a firing squad led by Belgian contract officers.

But Mr. Tshisekedi put aside those misgivings as the M23 began to resurge across eastern Congo in 2023. As Congo’s notoriously weak national army struggled to respond, he outsourced crucial parts of the fight to foreigners.

Romanians were tasked with defending Goma, the region’s biggest city, until they were routed in January 2025. Algerian drone pilots flew Chinese drones from Kisangani until their base was hit by a suspected Rwandan drone strike in May, current and former officials in the region said.

Those losses have left Mr. Prince as the pre-eminent military contractor in Congo — one who has embraced the language of colonialism.

In a podcast interview in 2024, he called on the United States to “put the imperial hat back on” in African countries that he said were “incapable of governing themselves.”

Asked if he was promoting a new form of colonialism, Mr. Prince replied, “Absolutely, yes.”

In interviews, Mr. Prince often plays up his tough-guy image, presenting himself as a hard-nosed pragmatist who is willing to harness the power of private military action. But in Africa, his ventures have often gone wrong.

In Libya, his mercenaries had to flee on a speedboat in 2019 after a dispute with the warlord who hired them. In Somalia, U.N. investigators accused his forces of violating an international arms embargo on Somalia in 2012.

In Congo, some fear more of the same chaos. Hiring Mr. Prince is a sign of the government’s desperation against the M23, but “it’s creating more problems than solutions,” said Zobel Behalal, author of a recent report on mercenaries in Congo. “It’s a sign that the army is very weak. And while others are making money, in the end it’s the population that suffers.”

Last month, Mr. Prince spent time promoting his new company, Vectus Air Defense Systems, which sells an anti-drone system that he says can protect oil fields, data centers and other sensitive sites. He also began negotiating with Congolese officials over a possible $200 million contract to protect the country’s air force assets, an adviser to the Congolese president said.

American officials say that Mr. Prince’s ventures in countries like Congo are entirely private and that he enjoys no U.S. government support. Still, Mr. Prince, who once donated $250,000 to a Trump campaign, uses his political connections to support his military operations. Mr. Prince’s sister, Betsy DeVos, also served as secretary of education during Mr. Trump’s first term.

Last January Mr. Prince traveled to Belgium for a meeting at the residence of the U.S. ambassador Bill White. In the meeting, Mr. Prince outlined his views on Congo to Belgium’s top Africa diplomat, Marc Pecsteen de Buytswerve, according to two European officials.

Then Mr. Prince asked for help.

His drones had been impounded at customs in the Netherlands and he needed to get them out. He also asked if Belgium would authorize the export of guns and ammunition from a Belgian manufacturer to Congo.

The State Department and Belgian foreign ministry declined to comment on the meeting, which State described as a “private diplomatic engagement.” But the answer to both of Mr. Prince’s requests, the officials said, was “No.”

Reporting was contributed by Eric Schmitt in Washington, Emanuel Stoakes in Christchurch, New Zealand, and John Eligon in Johannesburg.

]]>

item.title: An International Career Forged by the Struggles of Apartheid
item.description:
She lived her childhood in a slum without sewage or water, attended a school for only children of Indian descent, and knew that her skin color prohibited her from going to the beach her father would drive past during the Christmas season.

Navi Pillay, 85, was aware from a very young age growing up in apartheid South Africa what it meant to be stripped of her humanity, she explained in an interview with the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in 2019.

But she also described a pivotal moment that helped her rise from under the thumb of racism: Parents in her community in the coastal city of Durban pooled their money to send her to university, after her high school principal said she had potential.

That opportunity began a barrier-breaking career that led Ms. Pillay to becoming a lawyer, a judge on multiple international courts, the human rights chief of the United Nations and, on Friday, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate.

In announcing the prize, the Nobel committee said that Ms. Pillay had been “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.” She becomes the fifth South African to win the award, joining the ranks of the country’s most vaunted figures including Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

While much of Ms. Pillay’s global recognition comes from human rights work she has done abroad, her experiences in South Africa have indelibly shaped her life, and she has remained deeply invested in her home country’s sometimes-fragile democracy.

“I see this award as the voice of the majority of the world,” Ms. Pillay said in an interview with the South African state broadcaster on Friday. She added that a majority of South Africans “want the rule of law, they want the independent judiciary to be respected.”

Navenethem Naidoo, known as Navi, grew up in a community designated for Indians in southern Durban that was constantly under the threat of being declared a white area, which would have meant forced removal, said Saths Cooper, a friend and client of Ms. Pillay’s who is also of Indian heritage and grew up in Durban.

“We’d talk about the threats that were there but that our spirit is not going to be cowed by that kind of thing,” Mr. Cooper said, adding that they were determined to engage with communities far and wide to overcome the isolation that the apartheid government tried to impose.

Ms. Pillay’s father was a bus driver who wanted to ensure that she and her six siblings were not confined to menial labor, Mr. Cooper said. She was among the many young Indians in Durban who took up the struggle and embraced Black identity, in part countering the apartheid framing of people of color as “nonwhite.” Mr. Cooper said it was “a tool for mental liberation to identify as Black rather than a ‘non.’”

She studied law at what is now the University of KwaZulu-Natal. Because it was segregated, Black students had to attend classes at night, said Jessica Neuwirth, a human-rights lawyer and activist who has known Ms. Pillay for four decades. During the day, Ms. Pillay would go to the library, where she found books about the Nuremberg trials, helping inspire her fascination with international justice, Ms. Neuwirth said.

After earning her law degree in 1965, Ms. Pillay worked under a prominent anti-apartheid attorney of Indian descent, N.T. Naicker. She did much of his field work, like meeting with clients, because the apartheid regime had confined him to his home.

Ms. Pillay struggled to get hired by a law firm because of racial restrictions but eventually opened her own practice. She represented anti-apartheid activists and won critical rulings with creative approaches, Ms. Neuwirth said.

When the apartheid government locked up her husband, Gaby Pillay, who was also a lawyer, for political activities and cut off his access to the outside world, Ms. Pillay used his power of attorney to file an action on his behalf, Ms. Neuwirth said. She ended up winning an order prohibiting his torture.

In one case, she introduced the findings of the American psychiatrist Louis Jolyon West to argue that anti-apartheid activists who were tortured could not give credible confessions. The court sided with her argument, Ms. Neuwirth said.

Ms. Pillay was able to win due process rights for inmates on Robben Island, where high-profile anti-apartheid activists like Mr. Mandela were sent to solitary confinement.

She represented Mr. Cooper and several others after they were arrested for agitation during strikes in Durban in 1973. She allowed them to take an active role in shaping their defense rather than dictating their strategy, Mr. Cooper said. Consulting with the defendants and other activists who had faced similar charges, she crafted an effective, unified defense, Mr. Cooper said, and they were acquitted.

The apartheid government later put Mr. Cooper under house arrest. Though he was not a practicing Hindu, Ms. Pillay advised him to apply for an exception to go to temple, which was granted, Mr. Cooper said, and he got about three hours outside every Sunday.

Even as Ms. Pillay made strides as a lawyer, she faced constant indignities. In the Australian Broadcast Corporation interview, she described how, as an Indian lawyer, she had to use a separate entrance and sit at a different table from the white lawyers.

“I mean, what confidence can clients have in us when they could see that we were held in inferior position in the courtroom?” she said.

She recalled going to a magistrate’s office to speak with him, and when she entered he had his feet on the desk. “So you’re talking to the dirty soles of his shoes,” she said. “That’s what I mean about how humiliating it was.”

Ms. Pillay’s struggle to maneuver within a racist system applying unjust laws in some ways helped her develop the persistence she needed, she has said in interviews. She said in a podcast interview last year that she would keep filing legal motions even if they had little chance of succeeding because she believed that was the only weapon she had to fight the system.

“It was clear to me the only thing I can do is keep going, seeking justice,” she said.

She rose to international prominence shortly after apartheid ended in the 1990s, as a judge on the tribunal on the Rwanda genocide, which broke new ground in prosecuting the crime of genocide and treating mass rape as a form of genocide.

Ms. Pillay later served as a judge on the International Criminal Court, the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, and a substitute judge of the International Court of Justice.

She has also remained engaged in matters at home.

Ms. Pillay chaired a commission that looked into the challenges of migration in South Africa and presented a report to the government. With the United Nations, she launched an L.G.B.T.Q. equality campaign in South Africa. She was part of a tribunal that probed corruption in South Africa and made damning findings against the country’s leaders.

In 2021, she gave a lecture on human rights at Stellenbosch University and offered a searing critique of what she saw as some of South Africa’s failures to stand for human rights.

The Nobel Prize could bring new scrutiny to Ms. Pillay in part because of the bold stance she has taken on the plight of Palestinians. She chaired a U.N. commission last year that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Her receipt of the Nobel drew a strong rebuke from Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

But given where she came from, Ms. Pillay is unlikely to be deterred by critics, Mr. Cooper said.

During apartheid, Ms. Pillay had “a complete understanding of the dangers,” he said. “But also the practical ways to overcome those dangers.”

Zimasa Matiwane contributed reporting from Johannesburg.

item.title: A Week Later, Russia Hasn’t Said What Pathogen Killed Plague Researcher
item.description:
More than a week after a young plague researcher’s mysterious death from pneumonia, Russia has still not publicly identified the pathogen that killed her.

The possibility that the researcher contracted pneumonic plague in her lab led to global fears of an outbreak. Those worries have begun to recede as no other known cases have surfaced in the Irkutsk region, where Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old researcher at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died on Oct. 2.

But the absence of an official explanation for Ms. Shipilova’s death, despite thousands of tests conducted on others in the community and on her own remains, has stoked concerns about what, if anything, Russia’s authoritarian government might be hiding.

According to Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public health regulator, Ms. Shipilova’s remains did not test positive for any of the dangerous pathogens she was working on at the institute, which included the bacterium that causes the plague. The regulator has said she died of pneumonia of an unknown origin. Pneumonia can be caused by numerous viruses, bacteria and fungi.

The World Health Organization is still seeking to understand the “causative agent” of the fatal pneumonia, whether or not it was the plague, Maria Van Kerkhove, the W.H.O.’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, said at a news conference on Wednesday.

“If that is ruled out — they say that is ruled out — what did she actually die from?” Ms. Van Kherhove asked.

Experts said they believed that with modern testing technology, the Russian authorities should know the answer by now.

“Presumably, they have the capability within days to do a simple genome sequence,” said Raj Panjabi, who served as a White House public health official during the Biden administration. “Presumably, they’ve done that, but they’ve not shared the results, and that’s concerning.”

The lingering questions reflect a broader lack of global public trust that stems in part from unanswered questions about the origins of the Covid-19 pandemic.

More than six years after Covid upended the world, questions remain about whether the lab that was studying bat coronaviruses in the Chinese city where the pandemic started played a role in the outbreak. China swiftly rejected the possibility and impeded a global investigation into the matter.

In Russia, any possible case of a pathogen escaping a lab attracts outsize attention globally in part because the country is one of the few in the world that continues to work on biological weapons, according to the U.S. intelligence community’s annual threat assessment.

That has led to greater concern among officials and experts in the United States, who point to the nation’s vulnerabilities.

“The United States does not have a licensed plague vaccine,” said Andrew Weber, a senior fellow at the Council on Strategic Risks and a former Pentagon official in charge of biodefense. “Given that Russia has an illegal bioweapons program, it is very concerning.”

Ms. Shipilova was involved in testing which antibiotics and doses worked against Y. pestis, the bacterium that causes the plague, according to the summary of a study presented this year at a Moscow infectious disease conference.

The plague, which is endemic to Siberia and some other regions of the world, caused the “Black Death” that ravaged Eurasia in the 14th century, but it is treatable with antibiotics if caught quickly. Pneumonic plague is considered the most dangerous of the three main forms of infection, because it spreads from person to person and causes deadly, rapid-onset pneumonia.

Referring to Ms. Shipilova as “the patient,” the Russian authorities have said that she was vaccinated against the dangerous microorganisms she was working with, and that two reviews of the institute ruled out any “emergency situations” at the lab. The quarantine measures that the Russian authorities took in the Irkutsk region were put in place out of caution, owing to the nature of the patient’s work, they said.

Plague vaccines have long existed, but experts have raised serious doubts about their effectiveness and safety.

Beyond what pathogen led to Ms. Shipilova’s pneumonia, many other questions remain unanswered, including where she was in the days leading up to her death, what she was working on at the institute at the time, and how and when her illness first showed itself and then progressed.

Labs around the world working with deadly germs take extensive precautions to keep workers from being infected, but accidents have occurred.

Though Russia took swift action to quarantine and test individuals who had come into contact with the researcher, Rospotrebnadzor has not held any news briefings and has provided information only in periodic public statements. The Kremlin has declined to field specific questions, urging the public to listen only to public health officials.

Russia has been slow to reveal the details of other incidents with possible public health implications.

In 2019, Moscow concealed critical information about the failed underwater recovery of a nuclear-powered missile in the White Sea, which caused an explosion and left seven people dead. The authorities did not initially say that a nuclear device was involved, acknowledge a spike in radiation or warn doctors that they were treating irradiated patients.

Nondisclosure has long been the modus operandi of the Soviet and now Russian bureaucracy, said Alexander Kelle, a senior researcher at the Institute for Peace Research and Security Policy at the University of Hamburg in Germany. He cautioned against reading too much into the paucity of details.

“Just because there is a lack of information, we have to be careful not to equate that with something nefarious,” Mr. Kelle said, noting that there were many legitimate public health reasons for researchers to work on dangerous pathogens.

To posit any link to Russian biowarfare, he said, would “be stretching the very limited evidence that has been presented too far.”

In a video message on Thursday, the governor of the Irkutsk region, Igor Kobzev, sought to close the book on the episode. He said that the medical monitoring of people in the region had concluded and thanked his fellow Russian officials for taking swift action under intense scrutiny.

Mr. Kobzev said the W.H.O. had publicly confirmed that there were no risks to public health, though the organization has said it has not received enough information from Russia to make a risk assessment.

Some people commenting on Mr. Kobzev’s video in his Telegram channel weren’t having it.

“What caused the pneumonia that killed the healthy young woman?” one asked.

“Are there really still naïve, gullible people in our city who would believe this?” another commenter said.

A third wrote: “X-Files, nothing to see here.”

K. R. Callaway contributed to this report.

]]>

item.title: What to Know About the Delhi Protests
item.description:
The Indian police turned New Delhi into a fortress on Saturday as protesters tried to assemble in the city center to oppose a sweeping revision of the nation’s voter roll. The authorities took extraordinary measures to stop them.

A large number of officers have gathered and have erected tall yellow barricades around the protest site. Several protesters have already been placed under house arrest. Delhi-bound trains have been canceled. Officials ordered the closure of 45 metro stations.

The protests were called by a Gen Z movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party. The demonstrations follow a week of daily protests by opposition politicians and several activist groups who are expected defy a police ban and join Saturday’s rally.

Here’s what to know about the events in New Delhi, the capital of the world’s most populous democracy.

The protests stem from growing anger at a sweeping revision of the voter roll. The change, known as the Special Intensive Revision, began last summer as an effort to verify voter eligibility and remove duplicate or ineligible names. The government called it a long overdue push to clean up voter records.

It required Indians to submit multiple documents to prove that they were eligible to vote, and it ended up eliminating 130 million names. Critics said it had removed legitimate voters and forced people identified as dead to come forward to prove that they were indeed alive.

Critics have called the measure a politically motivated purge that could entrench the tenure of Prime Minister Narenda Modi, who has been in power for 12 years.

Leaders of Mr. Modi’s party reject the criticism. The home minister, Amit Shah, accused opposition lawmakers of “lies and disinformation” in a social media post. “Having lost their public support, these parties question institutions after every defeat,” he said.

The protesters say their goal is to ensure free and fair elections.

They have demanded the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar; an immediate halt to the voter roll revision pending an independent inquiry; and the restoration of the previous voter roll in coming elections.

A popular slogan by the Gen Z movement refers to the election chief by a diminutive form of his first name: “Gyanu. It’s done, bro.”

The anger at the election chief has been aggravated by news, reported by The Indian Express newspaper, that other officials within the election commission and the Supreme Court had expressed reservations about the exercise.

The protest was initially organized by the Cockroach Janta Party, a Gen Z movement that emerged this summer to decry a broken college entrance exam system. They won the rare ouster of a government minister.

Several groups said they would join the Saturday rally. They include farmers groups that led protests in 2020 against the government’s proposed agricultural reforms. They too marched toward central Delhi and faced a crackdown, but pushed the government to back down.

The opposition Aam Aadmi party, with which some Cockroach Party leaders had been involved, has also said that it planned to join, along with several leftist youth organizations. Those include the All India Students’ Association, affiliated with one of the country’s communist parties, whose members have led some of the most robust protests this week.

First, the irregularities in the voter roll revision has dented the reputation of the election commission, which for years had been seen as a credible institution that ran relatively fair elections.

Second, the protests reflect the force of the Gen Z Cockroach movement, which has been led by a handful of young people with no political experience and all under the age of 32. Their success regarding the college entrance system seems to have emboldened others both in the movement and outside it to speak out against the Modi administration.
